Ransomware Precursor 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

Overnight, a security rule fired on a Windows server. Read the alert before you touch anything — it is the only piece of information you are given for free:

The alert, in fullAn account authenticated from an EXTERNAL IP address. Then a series of suspicious processes was created on that host: one that READS lsass.exe (the Windows process holding credentials), and others that DELETE volume shadow copies and the backup catalog. Followed by large SMB transfers to internal file servers.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated right now, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know who broke in, from where, on which machine, exactly what they ran, where the data went, and when — and you will have a written report saying so.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge and no Elastic experience needed. The investigation itself is clicking and reading; the only typing is your report, at the end.
The pictures are realEvery screen picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, taken by screenshotting the real Kibana. Nothing is drawn from memory.
It never leaves you guessingAfter every click it says the exact number or text you should now be looking at, and a numbered circle points at the control.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux — and one removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon to save the whole guide as a PDF.

The screen pictures are real screenshots of this lab, running Kibana 9.1.0. Every word, button, column name, row count and timestamp in them is what your own screen will show. The numbers in this guide are not predictions — they were read off these exact screens, and the setup script re-checks every one of them against the live index each time the lab is built. The one thing you need first

Docker Desktop, installed and running. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker Desktop yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The attack

LSASSlsass.exe is the Windows process that holds users’ credentials in memory. Attackers “dump” it to steal passwords and hashes. procdump is the tool usually abused for it.
Credential dumpingReading LSASS so the attacker can authenticate as other users and spread sideways.
Recovery inhibitionVolume Shadow Copies and the Windows backup catalog are the victim’s way back. vssadmin and wbadmin manage them. Ransomware crews delete them first, so the victim cannot recover without paying. This is the single strongest ransomware-imminent signal there is.
SMBThe Windows file-sharing protocol, TCP port 445. Walking a file server over SMB is how an attacker finds the data to steal or encrypt.
Ransomware precursorThe steps immediately before encryption: steal credentials, destroy recovery, hunt for files. Catching it here is the entire point of this lab.

The tool

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* (294 records) and network-* (126 records).
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
DocumentOne single log record. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like source.ip. The part before the dot is the group.
KQLThe query language you type into Kibana’s search bar. field: value means “field equals value”, and and joins two conditions.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened, e.g. an IP address, an account or a file name.
True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The four fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by four fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record, which tells you what kind of thing happened. You need four of them:
    4624 = an account was successfully logged on  ·  4625 = a logon failed  ·  4688 = a new process was created  ·  event.category = the coarse split, authentication against process.
  • user.name — the account. The alert named one, and it is the pivot for the whole investigation.
  • host.name and host.ip — the machine, by name and by address. The alert named one.
  • process.command_line and process.target_name — what ran, and what it was aimed at. This is where the attacker’s intent is written in plain English, and it is the field that decides the verdict.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

This family of attack always has the same four beats: somebody gets in from outside, they steal the credentials held in memory, they destroy the victim’s ability to restore, and they start walking the file shares. Hold that pattern in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it, clause by clause.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, start it — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux — wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A black window that works through ten numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification every document in the auth data view = 294 every document in the network data view = 126 query 1 the authentication baseline = 268 query 2 the failed-logon dead end = 43 query 3 the external logon = 1 query 4 the staging processes = 3 query 5A the lsass credential dump = 1 query 5B the recovery-inhibition events = 2 query 6 the smb file-share traffic = 5 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those nine numbers are the answers to this whole investigation. The script has already proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-*

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “event.code holds a number” and “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data. If it had already loaded it, it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until the alerts are really there — 3 of them. If the rule had matched nothing, you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

Do this

  1. Read the Severity and Risk Score columns. Every row says critical, 99. The rule graded this as about as bad as it can.
  2. Read the Reason column on any row. It names the two things you were told and a third you were not: the event code, the account asmith and the host sec-win-04.
  3. Open one alert. In the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon — the two arrows pointing outwards.

What one alert says

Three tabs sit across the top of the opened alert: Overview, Table and JSON. They are the same alert shown three ways, and Overview is the readable one. It gives you the whole story in a sentence — the event, its host.name, its user.name, its source.ip and the highlighted fields that matched — plus the alert’s own timestamp and its status. Under Table you get the raw log record, with process.command_line in it.

Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule keeps running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September at 10:00 UTC. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the Alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the card after next, and it is not a fault.

Now read the rule’s own query

Go to Security → Rules in the side menu (on a narrow window the menu is the hamburger icon, top left) and open the rule that raised these alerts. It is named Credential dump and recovery inhibition on a flagged Windows host, and its Query field contains one line of KQL:

This is the rule's own query, and it is a walkthrough queryevent.code: 4688 and user.name: "asmith" and host.name: "sec-win-04"
Why that matters more than it looks

You will run exactly that line by hand in the Query 4 card, and it will return 3 documents — the same 3 the Alerts page is showing you. That is not a coincidence: the rule runs precisely this query, once a minute. So your alert count and your query count have to be the same number. If they ever disagreed, one of the two would be telling you a lie, and you would want to know which before you wrote anything down.

Two more things on that page worth noticing: Risk score 99, and the time window, which is the last 365 days. That long window is a lab-only concession so the rule can still match historical data — a real deployment would use a short window and alert on the shape of the staging set rather than on one host.

Pick the pile of logs you want

do not change it later2 min

There are two piles, and the alert is about both of them. For now, stay on auth-*, because the logon and the processes live there. You will switch to network-* in the Query 6 card, and you will find that switching is one click.

Do this

  1. Find the Data view dropdown: it is at the left of the search bar, and it already reads auth-*. Do not change it. Leave it exactly where it is for the next five cards.

Why the pile matters more than the query

You can write a perfect query and still get nothing, because you are looking in the wrong pile. There is no process field in the network records and no destination.ip in the authentication records. If a query of yours returns zero results, check this dropdown before you start rewriting the query.

“Managed” next to All logs

There is a third entry called All logs, marked Managed. It is one of Kibana’s own built-in views. It is not part of this lab, and using it will give you counts that do not appear anywhere in this guide. Ignore it.

Set up6

Open the time range, once, and then leave it alone

the single most important click3 min

Every number in the rest of this guide depends on this one step. Do it carefully, and do it only once.

Do this

  1. On the empty page, click the blue button Search entire time range in the middle of the screen. It is marked 3 in the previous card’s picture.
  2. The picker at the top right stops saying Last 15 minutes and starts showing a start and an end, joined by an arrow.
  3. Check the number in the tab. It must read Documents (294) for auth-*. If it reads anything else, stop and read the “If it breaks” card at the end.
  4. From now on, do not touch the time picker again. Not one more time for the whole investigation. Every count in this guide assumes this exact range.
Why not just pick a day by hand?

You could: open the picker, choose the Absolute tab, and type Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000 to Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999. But that range is expressed in your timezone, so on a machine eight hours ahead of UTC it would start at midday and quietly cut the first two hours of the day off your data. Search entire time range sidesteps the whole problem: it asks Elasticsearch for the first and last moment that actually has data, whatever timezone you are in.

The timezone rule, in one paragraph

The lab stores every event in UTC. Kibana prints timestamps in your own computer’s timezone, and in this version there is no setting that changes it. That is why the range in the picture above reads a clock time eight hours ahead of the stored value — the picker is telling you the same instant in your local time.

So: the counts are exact, and the clock times are local. Write down the times your own screen shows. Then lean on the gaps between events, because a timezone offset shifts every time by exactly the same amount and therefore cannot change a gap. Every timestamp in this guide is given as UTC with a note about what you will see.

Investigate7

Query 1 — the baseline

1 of 6 queries2 min

First we look at everything, to see the normal shape of a normal day. Every later query narrows this down, so this first one is your reference point.

Why you are running this query

You have 294 log records and no idea which ones matter. This query throws away everything that is not an authentication event, so what is left is just the logons, logoffs, failures and lockouts: 268 of them. The other 26 are process creations, which come later.

Without a baseline you cannot spot an anomaly, because you would have nothing to say what normal looked like.

Do this

Click inside the search bar, select whatever is there, paste in exactly this — including the double quotes — then press Enter:

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.category: "authentication"
What that number tells you

268 authentication events happened that day, in total. That is the size of the haystack you are about to search. It is also your control total — if a later query gives a number bigger than 268, you have made a mistake in the query, not found a surprise.

For scale: the busiest account has 70 events across the whole day, and the account in the alert has 4. Remember that ratio — it is the whole investigation in one sentence.

Next

Scary-sounding numbers are easy to find in a baseline. The next query deliberately produces one.

Dead end8

Query 2 — 43 failed logons, and why that means nothing

deliberate dead end4 min

Every security dashboard in the world has a red number on it. This card is about what to do when the number you find is red, and is not an attack.

Do this

Select the query in the search bar and replace it with this, then press Enter:

Windows event 4625 is “a logon attempt failed”event.code: 4625
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (43). Forty-three people failed to log on that day. That feels alarming, and if you stopped here you would escalate an incident that does not exist.

Now ask whose failures these were

Click the field name user.name in the left-hand list. A small panel opens showing the top values for that field across the records you are looking at.

This is a dead end, and knowing that is the skill

43 failures across 5 accounts, the worst account at 11, coming from 4 different source addresses over ten hours. That is not an attack. That is what an ordinary office looks like: people mistype passwords, caps locks stick, passwords expire on a Monday morning.

Failure counts alone can never prove an intrusion. If a rule had fired on “more than 40 failed logons” it would fire on almost every day of the year. This is why good detection rules are built on the shape of the activity — one account, one address, minutes apart — and not on a volume threshold.

What we have to do differently now

To find an attack in a haystack like this you have to stop counting all activity and start counting one account at a time. The alert gave us one: asmith. The next card follows it.

One tool that will not give you these numbers

It is tempting to click the Field statistics tab, just above Documents (43). It is a good tool and you will meet it properly in the Field statistics card — but it will not tell you “43 failures, five accounts, worst is 11”. It gives one row per field, not per value, and for user.name it says only “5 categories”. The panel you just used, and a filtered search, are the tools for counts.

Breakthrough9

Query 3 — follow the account in the alert

attacker isolated4 min

43 failures across five accounts proved nothing. So stop counting everybody and count one account: the one the alert named.

Why you are running this query

The alert named the account asmith. This query keeps only the successful logons for that account. Whatever is left is not a hunch and not a statistic — it is one specific event you can read, field by field.

Do this

Replace the query. Note the double quotes around the account name and the spaces around and:

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.code: 4624 and user.name: "asmith"
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (1). One successful logon. The count collapsing from 268 to 1 is itself a finding: it means 267 of those logon events had nothing to do with this account.

Open it and read the fields that matter

Click the ⇉ expand button. A panel called Document slides in from the right and shows every field of that one record.

What you now know

Who: the account asmith. From where: the external address 203.0.113.45. On which machine: sec-win-04, whose address is 10.0.4.20. When: read the @timestamp row — the value stored in the log is 2026-09-22 10:00:00 UTC, and the screenshots in this guide show it eight hours ahead of that. Write down whichever one your own screen shows.

That is four facts, and they are the whole opening scene of the incident.

Is that address unusual? Check, do not assume

Run this in the search box: source.ip: "203.0.113.45". The answer is Documents (1) — that is the only event from that address in the entire day, across the whole pile.

But it is not the only outside address in the data: 37 successful logons that day came from outside 10.0.4.0/24, spread over five external addresses (192.0.2.10, 192.0.2.24, 198.51.100.42, 203.0.113.9, and this one, with exactly one event between them). Knowing that stops you jumping to “external means attacker”. What makes this one different is what happened next.

The payload10

Query 4 — what they actually ran

the core of the alert4 min

Getting in is only the first third. Now we ask what the account did once it was on the machine.

Why you are running this query

Windows records every process start as event 4688. If we can list the processes that account started on the flagged host, we will have the rest of the alert in one table — and this is the same query the detection rule runs, so the answer here and the alert count have to agree.

Do this

Replace the query. This is the whole thing, three clauses, one line:

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.code: 4688 and user.name: "asmith" and host.name: "sec-win-04"
What you should see

Documents (3). Three processes. Nothing else, anywhere in the day, for that account on that machine — and the same three the Alerts page is showing you.

Now make the command lines readable

The Summary column squeezes everything into wrapped text, which is miserable for command lines. Instead, add each field as its own column: in the field list on the left, hover over a field name until a small ⊕ circle appears on its right, and click it. Do that for three fields:

  • process.name — the program that ran
  • process.command_line — the full command, which is where the intent is written in plain words
  • process.target_name — what the program was aimed at

Each field you add appears under Selected fields at the top of the list, and as a new column in the table.

What those three command lines mean

Oldest row — credential theft. procdump.exe -ma lsass.exe makes a full memory dump of the Windows process that holds every user’s credentials, and writes it to C:\Windows\Temp\l.dmp. The target_name column confirms it: lsass.exe. Whatever passwords and hashes were cached on that host are now in a file the attacker can read. -accepteula just means “yes I accept the licence” so the tool would not stop and ask.

Middle row — recovery inhibition. vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet destroys every Volume Shadow Copy on the machine. Those are the restore points a victim would use to get files back.

Newest row — recovery inhibition again. wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet destroys the Windows backup catalog. Shadow copies and the backup catalog are the two different ways to recover in Windows, and both have now been deleted within two minutes of each other. That is not housekeeping.

All three have the same parent process, cmd.exe — one command prompt, three commands, in sequence.

Why “delete the backups” is the scariest thing here

Most malware is after your data, because it can sell it or hold it for ransom. Malware that destroys the backups is telling you it intends to encrypt the data and stop you recovering it. When you see vssadmin and wbadmin run in sequence, the correct assumption is that encryption is minutes away, not days. That single judgement changes the urgency of everything you do next, and it is why this lab is graded as critical.

Next

You have read three rows and understood them. The next card turns two of those readings into numbers you can put in a report and check.

Prove it11

Query 5 — two counts for your report

3 of 6 queries3 min

“Three processes, two of which delete backups” is a claim. A claim with a number in it is evidence. These two searches are short, and they are the numbers your report actually quotes.

Check A — how many recovery-inhibition events?

Note the asterisks. process.command_line is stored as a single exact phrase, so a search for "delete shadows" finds nothing — the field holds vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, not delete shadows. Wrapping the words in asterisks means “contains”:

Search A — recovery inhibitionevent.code: 4688 and process.command_line: *delete*

The tab should read Documents (2). Those are your shadow-copy and backup-catalog deletions.

Check B — how many credential dumps?

Search B — credential accessevent.code: 4688 and process.target_name: "lsass.exe"

The tab should read Documents (1): the procdump.exe run against lsass.exe at 10:06 UTC. Across the whole day that is the only lsass.exe access recorded, and the only procdump.exe run.

A trap worth knowing about

Try event.code: 4688 and process.command_line: "delete shadows" and you will get Documents (0) and an error. Nothing is wrong with your data and nothing is wrong with your typing: process.command_line is an exact keyword field, so it matches the whole stored string or nothing. When a field holds a sentence, search it with asterisks at both ends (*delete*), or with the contains filter the sidebar offers when you click a field name.

Your evidence so far, in reportable form
1
successful external logon for asmith on sec-win-04 from 203.0.113.45
1
LSASS credential dump (procdump.exe → lsass.exe)
2
recovery-inhibition events (vssadmin shadows, wbadmin catalog)

Four claims, four numbers, each one produced by a query you can re-run and a count you can point at.

The target12

Query 6 — where the data went

4 of 6 queries5 min

The attack so far has been on one machine. Ransomware crews do not stop there — they go looking for the files. That last stage is in the other pile.

Step 1 — switch piles

Click the Data view dropdown at the top left and choose network-*. Two things will happen, and only one of them is a surprise:

  • The field list changes completely: 16 available fields, and network.bytes, destination.ip and destination.port appear for the first time.
  • The old query finds nothing, because event.code: 4688 and process.target_name: "lsass.exe" cannot match a connection record. The screen goes blank with “No results match your search criteria”. This is correct and expected — you are about to replace the query anyway.

Step 2 — ask for the SMB traffic from the compromised machine

Select everything in the search box and replace it with this, then press Enter:

SMB is the Windows file-sharing protocol, port 445network.protocol: "smb" and source.ip: "10.0.4.20"

The tab should read Documents (5). All five are on port 445.

Step 3 — add the two columns that matter

In the field list on the left, hover over destination.ip and then network.bytes and click the ⊕ on each. Every connection record has these, because a connection is defined by where it went and how much data moved.

Step 4 — sort biggest first

Sorting matters here, and there is a trap in it:

  1. Click Sort fields, just above the table on the right. A small panel opens showing the current sort — @timestamp, newest first.
  2. Click Clear sorting in that panel.
  3. Now hover over the network.bytes column heading until the small column actions button appears on the right of the heading, click it, and choose Sort High-Low.
Why clear the sort first

Because a sort added from a column menu is added to the existing one, not substituted for it. The old @timestamp sort stays first, all five timestamps are different, and the rows do not move — which looks exactly like the sort having failed. After you clear it, Sort fields reads 1 and the network.bytes heading shows a ↓.

What those five rows tell you

Two of the five transfers are roughly 15 to 18 times bigger than anything else this host sent that day, and they are the only SMB transfers in the entire dataset above 65,000 bytes — the largest anywhere else is 65,506. So these two are not part of the noise.

They go to 10.0.4.12 and 10.0.4.13, and both of those addresses appear exactly once in the whole 126-record network pile — in these two records and nowhere else. Nothing else in the day ever talked to them. An attacker walking a file server for shares to encrypt or exfiltrate looks exactly like this: two servers, a megabyte each, minutes apart.

And the times are 10:14 and 10:18 UTC — fourteen and eighteen minutes after the logon, four and seven minutes after the backup deletion.

Know the tools13

Field statistics — a good tool that answers a different question

reference3 min

Before the timeline, one short card about the second tab you have been ignoring. It is genuinely useful, and it is very easy to misuse.

Look at it

Go back to the auth-* pile with an empty search box, and click the Field statistics tab — the one immediately to the right of Documents, at the same height. It is a tab, not a section further down the page. Then click the small button beside Auto interval to hide the histogram, so the whole table fits.

So what is it for?

Use it to understand the shape of your data: which fields exist, what type each one is, how sparse it is, and how many distinct values it holds. That is genuinely how you discover that a field you assumed was always populated is not.

Do not use it for counts. If you need a number, filter and read the Documents tab, or open a field in the sidebar. “5 categories” is not “5 events”.

Two more things this card earns its keep for

First: for keyword fields the Distributions cell does count, and says so — “2 categories”, “7 categories”, “10 categories”. It is the number fields that get the min–max line instead. That inconsistency is what catches people out.

Second: the ⇅ chevron on the far left of each row expands that one field to a full chart. When you want to know the shape of one field, that is the right control — and it is how you would have seen, in one click, that process.name has 10 distinct values of which 23 are ordinary notepad.exe-type noise and 3 are the attack.

Put it together14

Build the timeline

the heart of the report6 min

This is the most important six minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file and write six lines, oldest first. The UTC column is the value as it is stored in the log. The on screen column is what the screenshots in this guide show, because they were taken on a machine eight hours ahead of UTC. Use whichever matches your own screen.

  1. 10:00:00 UTC  →  18:00:00.000 on screen
    Successful logon (event.code 4,624) for the account asmith on sec-win-04 (10.0.4.20), from the external address 203.0.113.45.
  2. 10:06:00 UTC  →  18:06:00.000 on screen
    Credential dump. procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe C:\Windows\Temp\l.dmp — a full memory dump of the process holding Windows credentials, written to a temporary file.
  3. 10:09:00 UTC  →  18:09:00.000 on screen
    Shadow copies deleted. vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet — every restore point on the machine.
  4. 10:11:00 UTC  →  18:11:00.000 on screen
    Backup catalog deleted. wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet — the second and last way to recover.
  5. 10:14:00 UTC  →  18:14:00.000 on screen
    964,221 bytes of SMB traffic (port 445) from 10.0.4.20 to 10.0.4.12 — a megabyte to a server nothing else in the day ever contacted.
  6. 10:18:00 UTC  →  18:18:00.000 on screen
    984,221 bytes of SMB traffic from 10.0.4.20 to 10.0.4.13.
The shape of the answer

All six events fall inside an 18-minute window on a single day, in this order: get in, steal the credentials, destroy the backups, then start moving megabytes off the host. The gaps are 6, 3, 2, 3 and 4 minutes — a person working steadily through a checklist, not someone poking at a box.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence and rules out routine administration. And because a timezone offset shifts every timestamp by the same amount, the gaps survive any timezone — which is why the pattern, not the clock, is the finding.

Then ask the questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer, and where it came from
Who started it?the account asmith — query 3
From where?203.0.113.45, external — query 3, the Document panel
On what?sec-win-04, address 10.0.4.20 — query 3
What did they take?1 LSASS credential dump — query 5, check B
What did they destroy?2 recovery-inhibition events — query 5, check A
Where did the data go?10.0.4.12 and 10.0.4.13, about 1 MB each — query 6
How long?18 minutes, 10:00 to 10:18 UTC
The one-sentence verdict

Between 10:00 and 10:18 UTC on 22 September 2026, an external address (203.0.113.45) logged on to sec-win-04 as asmith, dumped LSASS credentials with procdump, deleted both volume shadow copies and the backup catalog with vssadmin and wbadmin, and then transferred about a megabyte to each of two internal file servers, 10.0.4.12 and 10.0.4.13, over SMB.

That is a true positive, and it is a ransomware precursor. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the six queries you just ran.

Deliverable15

Write the report, then prove it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning

4. Impact

What is affected

the account, every machine involved, and the volume of data moved

5. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph

6. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out. Each one has to name a system — “monitor closely” is not an action

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Finish16

Tear the lab down

one file2 min

One file removes everything the lab created. Nothing is left running, and nothing of yours is deleted.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have exported your submission. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.
The list the teardown file prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container ransomware-precursor-001-elasticsearch container ransomware-precursor-001-kibana volume ransomware-precursor-001_esdata (this holds ALL the lab data) file .../ransomware-precursor-001/docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-ransomware-precursor-001

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. The five names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it will never touch

Every name in that list is derived from the folder name, and nothing else is considered for deletion. In particular:

  • No Docker images are removed. They are large and slow to download, so they are kept and the next setup is fast and works offline.
  • No other container or volume on this machine is touched, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files stay. The log data, the templates, rule.json and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

The teardown file never runs docker system prune and never removes an image. It says so on screen before it starts, and it means it.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives — including the detection rule and the three alerts. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not delete anything else looking for something to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference17

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Three things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing.

1. The screen is empty and there are no documents

Almost never a broken query. Check, in this order:

  1. Is the data view right? It must say auth-* for the queries up to Query 5, and network-* for Query 6.
  2. Is the time range right? If it says Last 15 minutes, the data is older than that and you will see nothing. Click Search entire time range again. This is by far the most common cause, and it happens after pressing F5 or navigating away and back.
  3. Is the query in the bar at all? It should be in plain text, not in a leftover filter row underneath.
If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the alerts page starts on Today while the log data is from September 2026. If the Alerts page is empty, set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the three come back. The alert card explains the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

2. The counts do not match this guide

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
Double every numberThe data was imported twice. Run the setup file with reset and then it again, which rebuilds the data exactly once.
Nothing for Query 6You are still on the auth-* data view. Query 6 has to run on network-*.
0 for the recovery-inhibition searchYou typed "delete shadows" instead of *delete*. The field is an exact keyword and holds the whole command string.
Times are hours offThat is your timezone, not a fault. Read the gaps, not the absolute clock times — see the Time range card.
Dates in the past, on a computer years aheadExpected, and not a fault. The log data is a real day in September 2026 and never moves. The rule that raises the alerts only looks back a year, so it keeps finding it.
The sidebar says 0 available fieldsStill a time-range problem. Click Search entire time range.

3. The lab will not start

What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker Desktop is not installed. Ask your instructor.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingOpen Docker Desktop and wait until it says Engine running, then run the file again.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run its teardown from the folder that owns it.
a container called ransomware-precursor-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied or moved, so a previous copy owns the container. The script shows you the details and stops without deleting anything. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run the teardown from the original folder first.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 294A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run setup-lab.cmd reset.
the rule is installed but has not produced 3 alertsThe rule only looks back 365 days. If your system clock is more than a year ahead of the lab data, change the clock or set "from" in rule.json wider and re-run.

Two controls that catch people out

  • Clicking a table row does nothing. You need the small ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. In the Document panel, Escape closes it. With a single result the next/previous arrows are absent, because there is only one document to step through — they are not missing.
  • The Field statistics tab shows one row per FIELD, not one row per value. It will not give you “11 and 8 each” style counts — for an exact number, run the query and read the Documents tab, or click the field in the sidebar.
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return a large number of documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.

How to use the screen pictures

Every picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, not a drawing. The numbered circles sit on the exact control they describe. Put your browser and the picture side by side, do the same click, and compare.

On a phone the pictures are wider than the screen. Swipe the picture sideways to see the whole of it.

One page deliberately has no picture: Security → Alerts. The rule that fills it is created by the setup script a minute before you look at it, so that page is given to you as an exact table of values instead of an invented screenshot.

Saving or printing

The printer button at the top right turns this whole guide into a single PDF with every card in order. The Copy button on each dark query box puts that query on your clipboard so you can paste it straight into Kibana. On the Write it up card, the EXPORT MY SUBMISSION button builds a separate PDF report out of what you typed.

The coloured markings

Yellow marks a value you must read off your own screen and write down — that is your work. There is deliberately no second colour: nothing in this guide is filled in for you, and no answer key is printed anywhere inside it. The answer key is a separate file that is not part of the student archive.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of three causes, and all three are on the If it breaks card near the end: the time range reset, the wrong data view, or Docker not running. Go there rather than guessing.
